A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OT-Transformer work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reorganization and additions in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on classification, sentiment analysis, and text generation, with numerical results and learning curves in Section 6 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds corruption tests, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements, and language-model metrics in Section 5 and Appendices B, C, and I.

M1.justification: The Transformer-parametrized dynamics, OT velocity regularization, and discretized training procedure in equations (7)–(9) remain unchanged. The new side-by-side pseudocode in Algorithm 1 documents the existing method rather than introducing a new component.

E1.justification: The original datasets and tasks are retained, but v2 substantially expands evaluation conditions: character replacement for nanoGPT, point dropout for ModelNet40, and Gaussian and uniform image noise for MNIST. These introduce explicit corrupted-input scenarios across text, point clouds, and images.

E2.justification: The original accuracy/loss comparator sets, including the N-ODE Transformer comparisons, are retained. The new nanoGPT timing comparison includes a Standard Continuous-time Transformer alongside the baseline and OT-Transformer (v2 Table 4), extending comparator participation in that experiment.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled test-time corruption levels and nanoGPT sweeps over regularization strengths from 0.01 to 5 and integration-step counts from 1 to 20. Evaluation also expands to perplexity, BERTScore, BLEU, ROUGE, and iteration time. The reported configurations and training budgets of the original experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's regularization comparisons and learning curves, v2 directly tests robustness to four corruption types and sensitivity to regularization strength and integration steps (Tables 3 and 5). These address whether the stability benefits survive input corruption and depend on particular hyperparameter choices.

E5.justification: The retained experiments keep their three- or five-trial mean/standard-deviation reporting and the single seeded OpenWebText trial. The new sensitivity study follows the existing three-trial practice. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: OpenWebText OT-Transformer best/final losses change from 3.02/3.03 to 2.90/2.91, while baseline values remain 3.20/3.21, without a stated configuration change. v2 also adds substantial corruption, sensitivity, timing, and language-metric results. For example, at 10% character replacement, Table 3 reports losses of 4.60 for the baseline and 2.42 for OT-Transformer.

T1.justification: The distributional-robustness proof in v1 Appendix E.1/v2 Appendix H.1 corrects an equality to an inequality when applying the Lipschitz bound after equation (78). v2 also specifies 1-Lipschitz functions in the Kantorovich-duality discussion. The principal theorems, assumptions, and remaining derivations are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract's advertised GPT-2 final-loss reduction increases from 5.6% to 9.3%, and the introductory Table 1 caption adds superiority across the newly reported language-model metrics. The central contributions concerning optimal control, plug-and-play integration, robustness, generalization, and parameter efficiency remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit computational-overhead tradeoff and explains mitigation through smaller models and fewer integration steps (Appendix B). It also interprets lower perplexity as lower predictive uncertainty and argues that the sensitivity results reduce the need for tuning. The existing theoretical applicability limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v1 promises code release upon publication; v2 states that code is public and supplies a repository address. v2 also adds forward-propagation pseudocode and measured per-iteration runtime. Most previously documented architectures, hyperparameters, training budgets, and GPU specifications are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds seven references covering corruption protocols, language-generation evaluation, and Transformer stability under layer normalization. Appendix A adds a short discussion of the latter work. The existing positioning relative to N-ODE Transformers, OT-based continuous normalizing flows, and other theoretical analyses remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from main-text Section 5 to Appendix A, and subsequent sections are renumbered. New explanatory appendices and a NeurIPS checklist expand the document, alongside localized wording, caption, affiliation, and acknowledgement edits. Most existing prose and the central narrative are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds robustness, runtime, sensitivity, and noisy-text perplexity tables, a perplexity illustration, and side-by-side algorithm pseudocode. The nanoGPT and OpenWebText tables gain metric columns, substantially changing their displays. Existing experimental tables and figures are also repositioned within the reorganized appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for a central claim: v1 inferred empirical robustness largely from clean-test performance, whereas v2 directly evaluates corrupted text, images, and point clouds. Sensitivity tests and runtime measurements also make tuning dependence and computational costs assessable, while pseudocode and code-access information improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, notably the unexplained clean-data perplexity differences between Tables 10 and 11.
